title: Mexico supplier payments for US companies: what to set up first
summary: How US companies should structure Mexico supplier payments: beneficiary data, USD/MXN conversion, SPEI, proof, timing, and backup routes.
body_text: For a US company, paying suppliers in Mexico becomes easier when the payment is treated as a repeatable process instead of a last-minute transfer. The company needs to know where the dollars start, when pesos are needed, which beneficiary receives them, and what proof closes the loop. This matters because supplier payments are tied to operations. A delayed payment can hold up inventory, customs support, carrier release, payroll support, or a local vendor that needs confirmation before continuing work. Start with the payment job Before choosing a rail, name the job: Is this a one-time large payment or a recurring supplier cycle? Does the supplier need MXN, USD, or either? Is speed more important than fee control? Does the supplier need proof before releasing goods or service? Does your team need an audit trail for reconciliation? The answer changes the route. A SWIFT wire may be fine for a large occasional payment. A repeat weekly supplier cycle may need a cleaner local-payout workflow. The setup checklist A reliable Mexico supplier payment process needs these pieces: Piece Why it matters Beneficiary legal name Prevents mismatches and reconciliation confusion CLABE and bank Needed for local MXN SPEI payments Invoice currency Determines whether conversion is part of the payment FX rule Prevents disputes over USD invoices paid in MXN Proof requirement Tells the team what must be sent after payment Cutoff awareness Keeps urgent payments from missing the bank window Reconciliation owner Avoids payment proof living only in screenshots If any of these are missing, the payment may still go out, but the operation becomes harder to manage. Why the US bank alone may not be enough A US bank is often the right place to hold dollars, receive customer funds, and run treasury controls. But it may not be optimized for repeated MXN supplier payouts. International wires can work, but they may involve cutoffs, intermediary fees, less transparent status, and manual follow-up. That does not mean the bank is wrong. It means the payment job includes steps around the bank: conversion, local payout, proof, and operating visibility. A better operating model A strong Mexico supplier payment setup usually has: A known USD funding source. A defined rule for when to convert to MXN. Saved and verified Mexican beneficiaries. A local peso payout path, usually SPEI. A shared record of status and comprobantes. A backup plan for urgent or after-hours payments. This model lets the finance team move from “Can we send this?” to “Which approved route should we use today?” How Coba helps Coba Banking is designed as an operating layer for companies moving money between USD and MXN. Where supported, a company can keep its existing US bank relationship, use Coba for the recurring USD-to-MXN payment workflow, and pay Mexican suppliers locally by SPEI. The practical value is not only the FX rate. It is fewer manual steps, clearer status, saved beneficiaries, and a workflow that maps to how cross-border businesses actually operate. When to look at Coba Consider Coba when your team regularly says: “The supplier needs pesos today.” “The bank cutoff already passed.” “Where is the comprobante?” “Who approved this beneficiary?” “Can we pay from our US dollars without rebuilding this each time?” Those are signs that the issue is not a one-time transfer. It is a payment mechanism your business now needs to operate reliably. See Coba’s supplier-payment flow or request pricing .

title: Why No Recruiters Message You on LinkedIn (and How to Get Found)
summary: You are not being rejected, you are invisible. Recruiters search LinkedIn by title, keywords, skills, and location. Here is how to surface in their search.
body_text: Why do no recruiters message me on LinkedIn? Because they cannot find you. That is different from being turned down. A recruiter with a role to fill opens LinkedIn Recruiter and types a search: a job title, a couple of skills, a city. LinkedIn hands back the profiles that match those exact words. Yours has to carry them or it never loads into the list, however strong your background is. So the fix is not a wittier headline. It is putting the plain job title and the real skills recruiters type into the fields the search reads first. You have the green banner on, or the quieter version of it. Eight years of real experience. A clean title, a headshot that does not embarrass you, a profile you actually finished. And the recruiter messages? Zero, three weeks running. That silence starts to feel like a verdict, like some recruiter pulled you up, squinted, and passed. Probably not, though. You were most likely never in the room to be weighed at all. Getting ignored and being invisible land in the same empty inbox, which is exactly why people mix them up, but underneath they could not be more different. Being ignored means a human opened your profile and moved on. Being invisible means you never came up in the search that a recruiter ran, so no human ever had the chance to reject you in the first place. The invisible version is far more common, and it happens to be the one you can fix in an afternoon. Recruiters search for you. They do not scroll for you Picture how a recruiter actually spends a Tuesday afternoon. Open req, impatient hiring manager, and a paid tool called LinkedIn Recruiter running on one monitor. They are not scrolling the feed hoping your face floats past. They type a query. A job title, a must-have skill or two, a location, maybe a target company, then enter. LinkedIn returns a ranked list of people who match. The recruiter works down from the top, messages a handful, and closes the tab. Twenty minutes, next req. That is the whole mechanism, and it is worth sitting with. The query they typed might literally read "Product Manager" AND "SQL" AND (Fintech OR Payments) , scoped to greater Chicago. LinkedIn here is not a social network. It is a search engine that happens to index people, and your profile is one page in that index. If the page does not contain the words in that string, it is not in the results. There is no slot labeled "qualified, just phrased it differently." You are not ranked low. You are not there. This is how the coworker with half your experience collects three recruiter pings a week while your inbox gathers dust. They are not the stronger candidate. Their profile just happens to be written in the language the search runs on, and yours is written in a different one. Read that back: the silence was never a rejection wearing plain clothes. It was a discoverability problem in a rejection costume. Once that clicks, the whole thing stops feeling personal and starts feeling like a to-do list. How LinkedIn Recruiter search actually works (the part nobody tells you) Here is the part that stays hidden from job seekers. A recruiter on LinkedIn Recruiter, or its cheaper cousin Recruiter Lite, does not type free text and hope. They build a query from a fixed set of structured filters and glue them together with Boolean logic. LinkedIn's own Recruiter Help lays out which fields the Boolean engine actually reads, and the list runs shorter than you would guess: job titles and location, the companies and schools on a profile, industries, spoken languages, and skills. Seven fields, give or take. A recruiter joins them with AND, OR, and NOT, or with the friendlier dropdowns LinkedIn labels Must have, Can have, and Doesn't have. That short stack of fields and operators is the whole vocabulary of the machine deciding whether you exist to it. In practice, a hunt for a mid-level marketer might come out reading like this: a current or past title of Content Strategist or Content Marketing Manager, SEO as a must-have skill, HubSpot or Marketo as a bonus, the whole thing pinned to commuting distance of Austin. LinkedIn takes that string, hands back every profile that fills the fields, and quietly drops the rest. There is no maybe pile. Now read that filter list one more time, because it doubles as a map of your own profile. Each filter is reaching for a specific field you either filled in or left empty: the title line, the location, the past employers, the listed skills, the school, the industry. Leave them blank, or pack them with words no recruiter would ever type into the box, and you have failed the filter before your actual experience gets so much as a glance. The cheering part is hiding in that same sentence, though. Every one of those fields is yours to edit this afternoon. Your headline and job title are doing the heavy lifting Go look at your headline right now. Is it a job title, or is it a vibe? "Turning coffee into code." "Storyteller. Problem-solver. Human." "Helping brands find their voice." Those read like personality, and to a keyword search they read like static. Nobody recruits for the title "Storyteller." If the words "Software Engineer" or "Content Marketing Manager" sit nowhere near the top of your profile, you do not come up when a recruiter searches those titles. There is no near-match consolation prize. Your name simply never gets generated into the list. Your headline is the most search-visible line you own, and your current position title sits right behind it. Both need to carry the standard, boring, searchable name of the job you want. Boring is the point here. Nobody is typing your metaphor into the search box. They are typing the title straight off the requisition, which came from HR, which lifted it from a job description that reads like every other one in your field. Match that, not your inner poet. You do not have to choose between findable and human. LinkedIn gives you 220 characters in the headline, which is plenty for the plain title plus the specifics that make you the right kind of that title. "Software Engineer at Northstar" tells a recruiter what you are. "Software Engineer | Python, AWS, distributed data pipelines" tells them what you are and hands the search four more terms to match on. Lead with the title, then load the value. If you want worked examples of that formula, our guide to writing a LinkedIn headline breaks down the patterns that pull recruiter clicks. Mirror the words recruiters are actually typing Here is the trap that catches genuinely qualified people. You describe your work in the words your last company used, and the recruiter searches in the words the market uses, and the two do not overlap. You wrote "team leadership." The recruiter typed "people management" and "staff management." Same job, same competence, three different phrases, and to a keyword search they are three unrelated strings. You do not surface, and you never find out why. The fix is unglamorous, and it works. Open three or four real postings for the exact role you want. Now read them like a spy, hunting the phrases that keep coming back: the tools, the titles, the responsibilities in the company's own words. Those phrases go into your headline, your About, and the top lines of your recent experience, but only where they honestly describe what you did. Why it works is almost too simple. The phrases a company writes into its posting are the same phrases its recruiters paste into the filter. You are not gaming a system. You are finally speaking the language of the people who are trying to find you. Two details make this sharper. First, spell out acronyms both ways, because a recruiter might search either. Put "Identity and Access Management" and "IAM" in your profile, "End User Computing" and "EUC," "Search Engine Optimization" and "SEO." LinkedIn maps some synonyms on its own, but do not gamble your visibility on it. Second, include the natural variants of your target title. "Senior Network Engineer," "Sr. Network Engineer," "Network Engineering." It costs you nothing and it catches searches you would otherwise miss. If you want to check whether your profile actually surfaces for the titles you are targeting, a free LinkedIn review will flag the exact gaps between your wording and the searches recruiters run. Not sure your profile surfaces for the titles you want? Get a free LinkedIn review that flags the weak headline, thin skills, and missing keywords keeping you out of recruiter search. Review my LinkedIn → The skills section is a search filter, not decoration Most people treat the skills list as a formality and stop at ten or twelve. That is a mistake, because Skills is one of the Boolean filters recruiters search with, and it is one of the cleanest ways to be matched. When a recruiter needs someone who knows Salesforce, they add the Skills filter and pull everyone who lists it. If it is not on your profile, you are not in that pull. You get room for up to 100, and Recruiter does not only read the ones you formally list. It scrapes for skills wherever they surface. A tool named once in your summary counts. So does something buried in an old job description, or sitting on a résumé you uploaded two years ago. It even infers a few on its own, so a mention of Tableau can register as data visualization without you ever typing the phrase. Useful, that inference, but do not build your visibility on it. The skills you formally list are the ones that map cleanly onto the filter, so those are the ones to choose with intent. The word that matters is relevant . Do not pad the list with fifty generic entries so it reads junior and diluted. Load it with the specific, in-demand tools and competencies for your target role. If you are a paid-ads specialist, the recruiter is filtering for "Google Ads," "Meta Ads Manager," "GA4," maybe "Klaviyo," not "Microsoft Office" and "Communication." Proficiency in the specific tool is often the exact thing that decides whether a recruiter even considers reaching out. Location is a filter most people set once and forget Location feels like a throwaway field. It is one of the first filters a recruiter applies, and getting it wrong quietly deletes you from local searches. LinkedIn's Recruiter documentation is specific about how it behaves: for an onsite role, the search returns people who live within roughly 100 miles of the chosen location, or who have signaled they are open to relocating there. For a remote role, location is not used to filter at all, so results can be global. Hybrid sits in between. The practical read is simple. Set your profile location to the metro area where you actually want to work, or to your target metro if you are willing and ready to move there. A missing location, a location set to a whole country, or a stale one from two moves ago can drop you out of the onsite and hybrid searches that make up a large share of roles. If you are open to relocating, LinkedIn has settings for that too, and using them puts you back into searches for cities you do not physically live in yet. "Open to Work," set to recruiters only, is a filter they actively use Open to Work has two settings, and people conflate them constantly. One shows the green #OpenToWork frame around your photo to everyone, your boss included. The other, the recruiters-only setting, shows nothing publicly and quietly tells LinkedIn Recruiter that you are open. For a working professional job-hunting on the side, recruiters-only is usually the right call. The reason it matters for findability is that "Open to work" is not just a badge. It is one of the Spotlights a recruiter can filter their search by, meaning a recruiter can pull up only the candidates who match the role and have privately raised their hand. When you turn it on for recruiters only, you move into a pool that recruiters deliberately fish in. The whole tired debate about whether the green frame looks desperate is beside the point here, because the recruiters-only setting never shows a frame. One honest caveat straight from LinkedIn: it "can't guarantee complete privacy," so a recruiter at your own company, using a personal account or connected to you, could in theory still see it. If you are worried about who else can tell you are looking, the reality of what LinkedIn's private mode actually hides is worth reading alongside this. The green-frame-versus-recruiters-only question deserves its own answer, and we have written the full breakdown of whether Open to Work helps or hurts . For findability, the takeaway is narrow: switch it on for recruiters, and you appear in a filter that surfaces the exact people who want to message you. Complete your profile, because empty fields are empty filters LinkedIn nudges everyone toward "All-Star" status, and it is easy to write that off as a gamified vanity meter. It is not entirely vanity. LinkedIn states plainly that a more complete profile improves the discoverability of your profile in search results. The reason is mechanical rather than mystical: the sections it wants you to complete are photo, location, industry, education, current position, skills, and a summary, and almost every one of those is also a field a recruiter can filter on. The photo is worth its own attention here, since it is the first thing a recruiter sees in the results, and a weak or missing LinkedIn photo quietly costs you replies. Look at that list next to the Boolean filter list from earlier and the overlap is nearly total. Location is a filter, industry is a filter, skills is a filter, your position title feeds the job-title filter, and your school feeds the schools filter. Completing your profile and making yourself searchable are not two separate jobs. They are the same job described twice, so every blank you fill is another search you can now appear in. That is a far better reason to finish your profile than a status meter. A dead profile reads as inactive, so keep it moving Recruiters have a Spotlight for this too. LinkedIn's "Active talent," sometimes shown as "more likely to respond," surfaces candidates who look active and reachable, and the behaviors it counts are concrete: you recently updated your profile, you shared a public résumé, or you applied to jobs through LinkedIn. A recruiter can filter their whole search down to just those people, because a candidate who edited their profile last week is likelier to reply than one who has not logged in since 2021. This is the documented reason behind a tactic recruiters use on their own profiles. Some flip a setting or make a small edit weekly, because a recent change signals activity and freshness. You can borrow it honestly: refresh a line, add a new skill, tidy your About every so often while you are searching. Treat it as staying current, not as a magic button that catapults you to the top of every result, because LinkedIn does not publish a ranking formula and the effect is a nudge, not a guarantee. What is documented is the direction. Recent, active, and complete beats abandoned. A bigger, relevant network widens who can even see you Here is a lever that gets dismissed as vanity but is quietly load-bearing. Not every recruiter is working from the same tool. Full LinkedIn Recruiter, the corporate version, can search the entire network and see everyone. But that license is expensive, often several thousand dollars a seat, so plenty of smaller firms and agencies run Recruiter Lite or Sales Navigator instead, and those cheaper tiers can only fully see and message people within your first, second, and third-degree network. To a recruiter on one of those tools, anyone past your third degree shows up as an anonymized "LinkedIn Member" they cannot even name, let alone contact. So growing your connections is not about hitting some round number for its own sake. It is about widening the circle of recruiters who can actually see you. Connect with people in your field, in the companies you would want to work for, in your target city. Every relevant connection expands the pool of recruiters on a cheaper license who now fall within reach of you. This is the one case where the "500+ connections" advice has a mechanism behind it rather than just social proof. Findable is not the same as flooded, an honest reality check All of this makes you findable. It does not promise you a full inbox, and it would be dishonest to pretend otherwise. Two truths sit alongside the advice. First, outreach volume swings wildly by field, seniority, and location, and none of it is under your control. A niche technical specialty in short supply gets pinged constantly. A clearance-heavy field, a hot skill set, a role in a growing industry, those inboxes stay busy. A generalist in a saturated field, or anyone job-hunting in a soft market where recruiters already have more applicants than they need, will see less no matter how clean the profile is. When employers can fill roles from the inbound pile, they source less. That is the market, not your headline. Second, being findable is necessary, not sufficient. It is the passive channel, the one that works while you sleep, and it runs alongside applying and networking rather than replacing them. A well-tuned profile means a recruiter with the right role can find you. It does not mean every recruiter will, or that the ones who do will always have a good job. Some of what lands will be a role paying 40 percent under your number, or one in a city you would never move to. That is normal. Screen it, ignore what does not fit, and keep going. Sourcing is only one lane of the process anyway, and it helps to see where it sits in how hiring actually works end to end. What is fully in your hands is whether you exist in the search at all. Silence with an optimized profile is the market, the same market that stacks hundreds of applicants on every posting. Silence with a hidden profile is a problem you created and can undo. And one thing paying LinkedIn will not fix is this: Premium does not make recruiters message you. It helps you reach out and see who posted a role. Plenty of people with no Premium hear from recruiters weekly, and plenty with Premium hear nothing. The lever is the profile, not the subscription. The make-yourself-findable checklist Run this the next time you have twenty spare minutes. In order of impact: Put the plain job title in your headline and your current position. Lead with the searchable title, then add the specifics. Kill the clever tagline that hides what you do. Mirror three or four target job descriptions. Pull the repeated phrases, tools, and titles into your headline, About, and top experience lines. Spell acronyms out both ways. Fill the skills section with the real, relevant, in-demand skills. You have room for up to 100. Use the specific tools a recruiter filters for, not generic filler. Set your location to the metro you want to work in, and turn on the open-to-relocate settings if a move is on the table. Switch Open to Work to recruiters only. No public frame, and you land in the Spotlight recruiters filter by. Complete every profile section to All-Star. Each blank you fill is another search you can appear in. Keep it current. Small edits and recent activity put you in the "Active talent" Spotlight and read as reachable. Grow a relevant network. It widens the pool of recruiters on cheaper tools who can even see you. Do the first three and you will have fixed most of the invisibility on their own. The point of all of it is the same: stop describing yourself the way you think of yourself, and start describing yourself the way a recruiter searches. If you want the broader, section-by-section profile guide beyond pure searchability, pair this with our full LinkedIn profile optimization walkthrough, and if you would rather flip the script and message recruiters directly, we have a guide to reaching out to recruiters on LinkedIn too. But the searchability piece is where the silent inbox actually breaks open. Frequently Asked Questions Why do recruiters look at my profile but never message me? A view without a message usually means you made it into the search but not into the shortlist. You surfaced, the recruiter clicked, and something on the page did not close the gap, or a stronger match came up two rows down. So treat a view as a near-miss rather than a snub. Look at whether your headline and current title carry the exact job title on the requisition, and whether your skills section names the specific tools the role wants. Tighten those and a lot of the silent views start turning into replies. Do I need LinkedIn Premium for recruiters to find me? No. Premium is a tool for your side of the search: reaching out, sending InMails, seeing who posted a role. It changes nothing about how findable you are when a recruiter runs their search. You will find people with no Premium fielding recruiter messages every week, and people paying for Premium hearing crickets. The lever that decides whether you come up is the profile, the title and keywords and skills and location. Fix those and keep the money. Does turning "Open to Work" off and back on really help? There is a real mechanism under the folk wisdom. A recent profile change feeds LinkedIn's "Active talent" signal, one of the Spotlights recruiters can filter their search by, so an edit makes you read as current and reachable. That is a genuine, free tactic worth using. What it is not is a button that catapults you to the top of every result. LinkedIn does not publish a ranking formula, and treating one weekly toggle as a cheat code overstates it. Staying broadly active and updated is the version that actually holds up. Should I use the green #OpenToWork frame or the recruiters-only setting? If you are employed and searching quietly, recruiters only is usually safer. It shows no public frame and still puts you in the "Open to work" Spotlight that recruiters filter by. The public green frame is more visible but tells everyone, including your employer. LinkedIn also notes it cannot fully guarantee that a recruiter at your own company will not see the private setting. We cover the full green-frame debate in a dedicated guide to whether Open to Work hurts you . How many skills should I list on LinkedIn? As many real, specific ones as you honestly have, up to the cap of 100. The skills section is a live search filter, not a checklist you tick off, so every genuine in-demand skill you add is one more search you can turn up in. Where people go wrong is padding. A list stuffed with "Communication" and "Teamwork" waters down the relevant skills and helps you nowhere, because no recruiter filters for those. Prioritize the exact tools and competencies your target postings keep naming. My location is remote. Does that hurt me in search? Depends entirely on the role a recruiter is filling. Remote searches ignore location, so a global result set works in your favor there. Onsite and hybrid are the catch. Those run a hard location filter, roughly a hundred-mile radius around whatever city the recruiter picked, and a blank or wrong location quietly drops you out. Set your profile to the metro where you want to be. Flip on the open-to-relocate options if a move is genuinely on the table, and you stay in both the local pool and the remote one. Does posting content on LinkedIn get me found by recruiters? Not in the way people hope. Recruiter search reads your profile fields, not your posts, so posting is nowhere in the documented ranking. Where it helps is the margins. Regular activity makes your profile look current, and a recruiter who clicks through to a page with recent comments and a live pulse trusts it more than a page that has not moved since 2021. Enjoy posting? Post. Just fix the headline, keywords, skills, and location before you write a single think-piece, because those are what actually put you in the search. Why does someone with a weaker background get more recruiter messages than me? Because their profile matched the search and yours did not. Keyword search has no opinion about who is genuinely better at the job. It just returns the profiles that carry the words the recruiter typed. So a thinner candidate whose headline says "Data Analyst" and lists "SQL" outranks a sharper one who called the same work "turning numbers into decisions." Annoying, yes. Fixable in an afternoon, also yes. Speak the recruiter's vocabulary and that gap closes fast, and ignore the insider myths about how LinkedIn secretly ranks you while you are at it. Do my number of connections affect whether recruiters can find me? Yes, more than the vanity-metric reputation suggests. The full corporate LinkedIn Recruiter license sees everyone, but it costs thousands per seat, so a lot of agencies and smaller firms run Recruiter Lite or Sales Navigator instead. Those cheaper tools can only fully see and message people inside your third-degree network. Past that, you show up to them as a nameless "LinkedIn Member" they cannot even open. Connecting with real people in your field, your target companies, and your city widens the ring of recruiters who can reach you at all. That is reach, not clout-chasing. I optimized everything and still hear nothing. What now? Sanity-check the target first. Pull up live postings for the role and confirm you actually match them, not the job you wish existed. If you do, the quiet is probably the market. Inbound volume swings hard by field, seniority, and how many candidates recruiters already have piled up, and a soft market means fewer InMails for nearly everyone. Keep the profile findable so the passive channel keeps working, then go do the active work it cannot do for you. Apply directly. Ask people for referrals. Message the hiring manager yourself. title: Intuit and Rehmann partner to fuel mid-market business growth with powerful AI-native ERP solution and advisory services
summary: Intuit Enterprise Suite provides growing businesses with enterprise-grade power and AI-driven intelligence that simplifies complexities, boosts productivity and profitability
body_text: Intuit Enterprise Suite provides growing businesses with enterprise-grade power and AI-driven intelligence that simplifies complexities, boosts productivity and profitability Rehmann provides transformative advisory services that deliver confidence with innovative solutions that maximize client potential Intuit Inc. (Nasdaq: INTU), the global financial technology platform that makes Intuit TurboTax , Credit Karma , QuickBooks , and Mailchimp , today announced a partnership with Rehmann , a professional advisory firm focused on accelerating client growth, to deliver Intuit Enterprise Suite to the firm’s growing list of scaling, mid-market businesses needing a powerful, AI-native, ERP solution that drives growth. Together, Intuit and Rehmann will deliver meaningful client services coupled with Intuit’s AI-native, intelligent ERP platform that simplifies the complexities of scaling, multi-entity businesses and automates workflows through a modern, intuitive experience. With Intuit Enterprise Suite, Rehmann will streamline its clients’ multi-entity accounting and reporting, and support those currently on QuickBooks with a seamless upgrade experience. The firm will also leverage the platform’s advanced artificial intelligence capabilities to assist with routine accounting tasks and quickly identify anomalies, enabling greater accuracy, efficiency, and insight. “Like Intuit, Rehmann is obsessed with customer success,” said Simon Williams, vice president, Accountant Segment, Intuit. “This partnership reflects our combined commitment to fuel business growth through the adoption of innovative, adaptable, AI-native solutions that streamline workflows, help save time, and deliver data-driven insights that drive faster decision making that accelerates profitability.” Today’s growing mid-market businesses are more complex. They’re often overserved by legacy ERP systems that are expensive, time-consuming, and costly to install and learn. M id-market businesses are also over-digitized, using up to 25 different apps to manage and run their business. This leads to a fragmented tech stack with data silos, resulting in limited visibility into business performance, a lack of integrated workflows, and an inability to make data-backed, confident decisions. Intuit Enterprise Suite is transforming how more complex, mid-market businesses grow, eliminating the need for companies to adopt costly, legacy ERPs or juggle multiple applications to manage their operations. It provides businesses with an adaptable, intelligent, AI-native ERP solution that includes multi-entity and multi-dimensional financial management capabilities, business intelligence and reporting, payments and bill pay, project profitability, payroll, HR, and marketing, in one connected, scalable, cloud-based platform . It also provides tailored workflows and reports and connects to an extensive partner ecosystem to create an optimized and customized experience that meets unique, industry-specific needs. "We’re excited to partner with Intuit on this journey," said Sharon Berman, principal, Finance and Accounting Solutions, Rehmann. "This strategic move underscores our dedication to innovation and operational excellence. With Intuit Enterprise Suite, we’re positioning our firm to deliver enhanced financial clarity and agility, supporting smarter decision-making and long-term growth.” About Intuit Intuit is the global financial technology platform that powers prosperity for the people and communities we serve. With approximately 100 million customers worldwide using products such as TurboTax , Credit Karma , QuickBooks , and Mailchimp , we believe that everyone should have the opportunity to prosper. We never stop working to find new, innovative ways to make that possible. Please visit us at Intuit.com and find us on social for the latest information about Intuit and our products and services. About Rehmann Rehmann is a professional advisory firm that provides accounting and assurance, business solutions and outsourcing, specialized consulting, and wealth management services. For over 80 years, Rehmann has provided forward-thinking solutions to our clients. With over 1,100 associates in our offices across Michigan, Ohio, and Florida, and those working remotely across the country, we are the momentum behind what’s possible. We focus on the business of business, allowing companies and individuals to focus on what makes them extraordinary. We help you look to the future with confidence, thanks to our unrivaled expertise and integrity. We’re a proud member of HLB International, a global network of independent accounting and advisory firms, and through our partnerships with our clients and communities, we drive impact that empowers our world. Find us online at rehmann.com and check out our 2024 Annual Report.

title: IBM and Qedma Demonstrate Quantum Advantage, Modeling Physics Beyond Classical Capabilities Through Trusted Quantum Computation
summary: Qedma Quantum Computing & IBM announced a breakthrough study demonstrating how trusted, error-mitigated quantum computation is possible, & can be used to explore the physics of materials beyond the capabilities of state-of-the-art classical simulations.
body_text: YORKTOWN HEIGHTS, N.Y. and TEL AVIV, Israel, July 30, 2026 – Qedma Quantum Computing , a pioneer in quantum error reduction software and IBM (NYSE: IBM ) today announced a breakthrough study demonstrating how trusted, error-mitigated quantum computation is possible, and can be used to explore the physics of materials beyond the capabilities of state-of-the-art classical simulations, including those run on one of the world's most powerful supercomputers. By combining Qedma’s advanced error mitigation software, QESEM, with IBM quantum computers, researchers observed complex and long-lived quantum dynamics in systems of up to 74 qubits. This enabled them to reach a paradigm where multiple state-of-the-art classical approaches failed to provide consistent, reliable answers. The results mark the first time quantum advantage has been achieved with commercially available hardware and software to establish error-mitigated, advanced quantum computers as trusted scientific instruments for exploring physics that could lead to better and ultrafast optoelectronics, light-induced superconductors, and other advanced materials applications. Exploring Physics at the Classical Frontier The collaboration investigated the subtle, oscillatory dynamics of a two-dimensional Floquet Ising model, which is a system that physicists use to study how a material’s magnetic properties evolve when rhythmically driven by external pulses. Understanding whether such oscillations persist in larger systems has remained an open challenge because the relevant regimes rapidly overwhelm classical computational methods. Using an IBM quantum computer, which is powered by the IBM Quantum Heron processor and available on the cloud, together with Qedma's Quantum Error Suppression and Error Mitigation (QESEM) software, which is also available on the cloud, the team was able to resolve these dynamics with precision. Beyond Leading Classical Methods To evaluate the significance of the quantum results, the team worked with RIKEN, Japan's leading national comprehensive research institute, and BlueQubit, a leading developer of large-scale quantum circuit simulation technology, to compare them against state-of-the-art classical simulation approaches that spanned fundamentally different computational strategies. As the system grew in complexity over time, none of the classical approaches could consistently agree at the scale reached by the quantum experiments, even when run on Fugaku, one of the world’s most powerful supercomputers. By contrast, the error-mitigated quantum results remained consistent and revealed clear, long-time oscillatory behavior. To enable continued classical benchmarking from the community, the team publicly released the quantum circuits and results to the Quantum Advantage Tracker , prior to the arXiv pre-print released this week. Building Trust Through Validation A defining feature of the study is its extensive validation strategy. The team first employed an unbiased error-mitigation protocol against classical calculations wherever such comparisons remained possible, before pushing the protocol to the point where these classical simulations lost accuracy. Then, they benchmarked a more scalable mitigation approach against those trusted results before extending to larger system sizes and longer evolution times. Independent validation was also performed across quantum hardware platforms, including trapped-ion systems from Quantinuum. The consistent behavior observed across technologies provided additional evidence that the measured physics originated from the simulated quantum system, rather than from device-specific or mitigation errors. “IBM quantum computers have reached a maturity where they can produce solutions that, for the first time, achieve both trust in the solution through extensive testing and outperform the best classical simulation methods. I look forward to seeing future results benchmarked through the Quantum Advantage Tracker as we deepen our understanding of the boundary between quantum and classical computation,” said Jay Gambetta, Director of IBM Research and IBM Fellow . “By combining IBM’s quantum computers with Qedma's advanced error reduction technology, we are transforming quantum computing into a practical tool to expand the frontier of knowledge.” “For decades, quantum computing has promised discoveries beyond the reach of classical computers. Today, we're beginning to see that promise become reality,” said Dr. Asif Sinay, CEO and co-founder of Qedma . “By leveraging Qedma’s software to make today's quantum computers significantly more powerful and reliable, we're helping move the quantum computing industry closer to real-world, commercial impact.” “Quantum computers are beginning to open new possibilities for scientific discovery within the high-performance computing environment,” said Dr. Mitsuhisa Sato, Division Director of the Quantum-HPC Hybrid Platform Division, RIKEN Center for Computational Science . “This work leveraged RIKEN’s leadership in advanced classical simulation and supercomputing, alongside Qedma’s error mitigation software on IBM quantum computers, to demonstrate the ability of quantum computing to surpass the capabilities of leading classical methods. It is an important step towards a future where quantum and classical computing work together to advance science.” Qedma’s advanced error reduction software, QESEM, available in the Qiskit Functions Catalog on the IBM Quantum Platform, mitigates the impact of noise present in today's quantum computers. Rather than waiting for large-scale, fully fault-tolerant quantum computers, QESEM’s patented approach unlocks the ability to execute larger and more complex quantum workloads while producing more accurate results. The software offers various error mitigation methods, including an unbiased approach which provides guaranteed accuracy in extracting reliable results from noisy quantum hardware. It is currently being used by leading enterprises, academic institutions, and research laboratories around the world. More Announcements of Quantum Advantage Emerge Today, alongside this milestone from IBM and Qedma, partners from across IBM’s ecosystem are announcing demonstrations of quantum advantage. To learn more, visit https://www.ibm.com/quantum/blog/quantum-advantage . About Qedma Quantum Computing Qedma is accelerating the path to practical quantum computing by dramatically reducing the impact of hardware errors. Its hardware-agnostic software, QESEM, enables researchers and enterprises to run larger and more complex quantum algorithms while obtaining more accurate and reliable results on today’s quantum computers. By overcoming one of the biggest barriers facing the industry, Qedma helps unlock scientific discoveries and enables users to push beyond the limits of current quantum hardware. Qedma was founded by Dr. Asif Sinay together with two prominent scientists: Prof. Dorit Aharonov, who thirty years ago proved that error corrected quantum computation is possible and laid the foundations of quantum fault tolerance, and Prof. Netanel Lindner, a world-renowned theoretical condensed matter physicist known for his work on complex quantum systems. For more information, visit www.qedma.com . About IBM IBM is a leading provider of global hybrid cloud and AI, and consulting expertise. We help clients in more than 175 countries capitalize on insights from their data, streamline business processes, reduce costs and gain the competitive edge in their industries. Thousands of governments and corporate entities in critical infrastructure areas such as financial services, telecommunications and healthcare rely on IBM's hybrid cloud platform and Red Hat OpenShift to affect their digital transformations quickly, efficiently and securely. IBM's breakthrough innovations in AI, quantum computing, industry-specific cloud solutions and consulting deliver open and flexible options to our clients. All of this is backed by IBM's long-standing commitment to trust, transparency, responsibility, inclusivity and service. Visit www.ibm.com for more information. Flywire Research: Finance Leaders Say AI Will be Essential… | Flywire
summary: Flywire's survey of 300+ finance professionals highlights the critical need for AI-enabled, integrated A/R automation to combat increasing workloads and…
body_text: July 31, 2026 Flywire Corporation (Flywire) (Nasdaq: FLYW), a global payments enablement and software company, released a report, “ Beyond Automation: What Finance Leaders Really Need from AI ,” uncovering the state of Artificial Intelligence (AI) readiness within the office of the CFO. Based on a survey of over 300 finance professionals at U.S. companies, the findings reveal a sector at a tipping point: while 99% of respondents believe at least some part of finance will rely on AI within five years, and have budgeted for AI tools, they want to make sure their investments have a real and lasting impact. They do not want to add more complexity, as it is apparent from respondents that right now, one of the chief bottlenecks to getting paid faster is the fact that the process lives in several different systems, and hinders them from working in a more strategic capacity. As workloads increase and headcounts remain flat, 92% of finance leaders report a rise in accounts receivable (A/R) volume over the past year. Manual processes are the biggest bottleneck - specifically data entry (26%), following up on overdue invoices (26%), and cash application (25%). 83% say poor integration and a lack of visibility across A/R systems are their biggest challenges. “ Finance leaders are ready to embrace AI, but they are rightfully cautious about how to implement it effectively ,” said Chris Couch, Head of Product, B2B, Flywire. “ The data shows that ‘bolt-on’ tools are creating more complexity, not less. What these teams need is embedded, reasoning AI that acts on their behalf, identifying exceptions and matching payments with human oversight, freeing them up for more strategic work.” Key Findings from the Report: A Growing Reliance on AI: 64% of finance leaders say AI will be important or essential to staying competitive in the next two years. Budgeting is already following this sentiment, with 90% of respondents having already allocated funds for AI-enabled tools. The "Bolt-On" Burden: Fragmented systems are a primary culprit for inefficiency. 83% of leaders cite poor integration between A/R processes and systems of record as a major challenge. More than half of companies using enterprise or accounting software like NetSuite, Xero, or QuickBooks are "bolting on" up to four different tools to manage A/R. The AI Wishlist: Leaders are looking for AI that does more than follow preset rules. The most sought-after capabilities include automating payment matching (98%), real-time cash flow forecasting (96%), and auto-configuring workflows (97%). The Trust Gap: Despite the enthusiasm, barriers remain. 39% of respondents cite a lack of trust or transparency as their top concern for using AI in collections, followed by concerns over accuracy (37%) and data privacy (34%). Flywire’s AI-Powered Invoice-to-Cash: The Strategic Solution Invoiced, Flywire’s AI-native Invoice-to-Cash platform , is uniquely positioned to solve the challenges identified in the survey by providing a single, fully integrated platform that automates the entire A/R lifecycle. By embedding AI functionality directly into the A/R workflow, Flywire enables businesses to: Reduce Payment Friction: Send invoices with embedded payment options, allowing global customers to pay in their preferred currency and method. Behind the scenes, a combination of AI technology and people are ensuring the highest levels of transaction security. Eliminate Manual processes: AI-enabled cash matching streamlines cash application to minimize reconciliation errors, reducing administrative burden and increasing visibility. Scale Without Headcount: Integration with the system of record ensures no one is minding multiple systems, and teams can focus on strategic financial management rather than repetitive data entry. Smart chasing automates the dunning process to free up time and speed payments. Finance gets real-time cash flow insight to speed financial close. “ The role of the finance professional is shifting from repetitive task management to strategic oversight ,” continued Couch. “ Our goal is to provide the 'AI fuel' that understands a company's specific customer history and relationship nuances, delivering a localized and effortless experience for both the payer and the receiver. Resources Download the full report, Beyond Automation: What Finance Teams Really Need from AI . About Flywire Flywire is a global payments enablement and software company. We combine our proprietary global payments network, next-gen payments platform and vertical-specific software to deliver the most important and complex payments for our clients and their customers. Flywire leverages its vertical-specific software and payments technology to deeply embed within the existing A/R workflows for its clients across the education, healthcare and travel vertical markets, as well as in key B2B industries. Flywire also integrates with leading ERP systems, such as NetSuite, so organizations can optimize the payment experience for their customers while eliminating operational challenges. Flywire supports more than 5,100 clients with diverse payment methods in more than 140 currencies across 240 countries and territories around the world. Flywire is headquartered in Boston, MA, USA with global offices. For more information, visit www.flywire.com . Follow Flywire on X (formerly known as Twitter), LinkedIn and Facebook . title: How to Turn a Spreadsheet Into an App: Complete Guide (May 2026)
summary: Learn how to turn a spreadsheet into an app in May 2026. Step-by-step guide covering data cleanup, tool selection, workflow migration, and interface design.
body_text: Spreadsheets hit a wall once your team grows or your data gets complex. You're stuck copying files around, dealing with version conflicts, and manually updating people who need live information. The solution is converting your Excel or Google Sheet into an app that handles permissions, automation, and real-time access. This guide walks you through exactly how to convert your spreadsheet , including data cleanup, tool selection, workflow migration, and interface design that actually fits how your team works. TLDR: Spreadsheets fail when multiple users need access, lacking permissions and version control Clean your data before conversion: remove merged cells, standardize formats, label columns AI app builders work best for non-technical teams needing fast, custom workflows Start by migrating one critical workflow, test it, then expand to avoid breaking everything Stacker builds working apps from plain language and syncs with your existing spreadsheet data Why You Should Turn Your Spreadsheet Into an App Spreadsheets are a great starting point, but they were built for personal analysis, not team collaboration or shared workflows. Once your data grows or more people need access, the cracks start to show . Here are some of the most common pain points that push teams to make the switch: Version control becomes a nightmare when multiple people edit the same file, leading to conflicts and lost data. There are no user permissions, so anyone with access can see or edit everything, including data they shouldn't be able to access. Spreadsheets break under pressure, especially with large datasets, leading to slow load times, formula errors, and crashes. Sharing data externally with clients or vendors means emailing files back and forth with no audit trail. There is no real-time visibility, so stakeholders can't check live data without someone manually sending an update. Turning your spreadsheet into an app solves these issues by giving you a structured interface, proper access controls, and a single source of truth your whole team can rely on. Understanding When Spreadsheets Reach Their Limits Spreadsheets are genuinely useful for a wide range of tasks, but they have a ceiling. Once your data grows, your team expands, or your processes get more complex, that ceiling becomes hard to ignore. Some of the most common signs your spreadsheet has hit its limit: Multiple people need to edit the same file at once, leading to version conflicts and overwritten data. You're manually copying data between sheets or sending files back and forth over email. Non-technical users make formatting errors that break formulas or corrupt your data. There's no way to control who sees what, so sensitive information gets exposed to the wrong people. The file has grown so large it loads slowly or crashes entirely. At this point, a spreadsheet stops saving you time and starts costing it. Converting your Excel or Google Sheet into an app gives you the same underlying logic with a proper interface, access controls, and the ability to scale. Document Your Spreadsheet's Jobs to Be Done Before picking a tool or copying any data, document what your spreadsheet actually does. Not what it contains, but what jobs it performs for your team. Walk through these questions: What tasks do people perform each time they open the file? Are they entering data, running lookups, or updating statuses? Where are the decision points? What information triggers an action or a change in status? What does the spreadsheet produce in the end? Reports, a ranked list, an approval queue? Who needs access, and does everyone need to see the same information? The answers become the blueprint for your app . Skip this step, and you risk rebuilding the same spreadsheet in a new container, which solves nothing. A good app is a purpose-built workflow , not a replica of what you already have. Clean and Structure Your Data for App Migration Before any conversion tool can reliably read your spreadsheet, the data in it needs to be clean and consistently structured. Messy formatting, merged cells, and scattered logic are among the most common reasons app migrations fail or produce broken outputs. Here are the most important things to fix before you start: Remove merged cells and split them into individual rows or columns, since most conversion tools cannot parse merged layouts correctly. Standardize data types within each column so dates are formatted consistently, numbers are not stored as text, and dropdown values are consistent. Move formulas to clearly labeled columns and document any logic that the app will need to replicate. Delete any blank rows or columns used purely for visual spacing, as these can disrupt how tools detect your data range. Give every column a clear, unique header in row one, with no empty header cells. Cleaning your spreadsheet before conversion will save you time debugging the output afterward. Choose the Right Tool for Your Spreadsheet Conversion The right approach depends on three factors: your team's technical skill level, your timeline, and how much customization you actually need. Approach Best for Key tradeoff AI app builder Non-technical teams that want to describe and build Output quality depends on how clearly you define requirements No-code with data sync Teams keeping Airtable, Sheets, or similar tools intact Works best for simpler data models Database migration tool Moving off spreadsheets permanently Requires upfront data modeling work Custom development Highly unique or compliance-driven workflows Higher cost and longer build time For most small and mid-sized teams, an AI app builder covers the full range of requirements without the cost or complexity of custom development. How to narrow down your choice A few questions worth asking before committing to any tool: How often does your data structure change? Frequent schema changes are harder to manage once you migrate to a database. Who needs to access the app? External users typically require proper permissions and authentication that spreadsheets can't handle. Do you need offline access or mobile support? Some tools export to Android or iOS; others are web-only. Answering these honestly will save you from picking a tool that fits today but breaks under next quarter's requirements. Move Your Workflow and Data Into Your New App Start with your most critical workflow, not your entire dataset. Migrate one process, test it thoroughly, then expand from there. The core steps: Import your cleaned data into the app's database tables, mapping each spreadsheet column to the correct field type so nothing gets lost in translation. Recreate key calculations as formula fields or workflow logic inside the app, replacing any formulas that previously lived in hidden spreadsheet cells. Set up user roles so clients, vendors, and admins each see only what they need, keeping sensitive data protected by default. Configure automation for repetitive tasks like status updates or email notifications so your team stops doing manual work that the app can handle on its own. Run both systems in parallel for the first week or two. You'll catch gaps before anyone outside your team notices them. Build the Right Interface for Your Users Once your data is in the app, resist the temptation to recreate your spreadsheet row by row. The interface is where the real upgrade happens. Think in terms of who's looking at what: Internal team members need filtered table views, status boards, and quick-access forms with built-in validation. External clients or vendors need filtered views showing only their own records, with no access to the broader dataset. Managers and admins need summary dashboards that automatically roll up key numbers, instead of requiring someone to compile them manually. Forms deserve special attention here. Unlike a spreadsheet cell, a form field can enforce the right data type, flag missing values, and stop errors before they enter your system at all. Check how the app displays on mobile, too. Spreadsheets are nearly unusable on phones. A well-built app should work wherever your users actually are. Turn Your Spreadsheet Into a Stacker App With AI If you've worked through the steps above, you already have everything Stacker needs to get started. Describe what your spreadsheet does in plain language, and the AI builds a working app around it. Permissions, hosting, and authentication are included from the start. For teams staying on Google Sheets, Airtable, or Notion, Stacker syncs in two directions. Your existing data stays where it is. Stacker puts a proper app interface on top, with role-based access and real-time updates, without requiring you to move anything. Stacker focuses on business app patterns , so you can describe your workflow, refine it through conversation, and get your app live at yourapp.stacker.app. No developer required. Final Thoughts on Spreadsheet to App Migration Spreadsheets weren't designed for team collaboration and complex workflows. When you convert your spreadsheet to a web app , you're giving your existing work a structure that can scale with your team. Focus on cleaning your data first, then move your most critical workflow before touching anything else. Book a demo to talk through how your specific spreadsheet could work as an app. FAQs Can I turn a spreadsheet into an app without learning to code? Yes. AI app builders let you describe what you need in plain language and generate a working app from your spreadsheet data. You skip the technical learning curve and get a functional app with permissions, hosting, and authentication already built in. What's the best way to convert an Excel spreadsheet to a web application for free? Start by cleaning your spreadsheet (remove merged cells, standardize data types, label all columns clearly), then use an AI app builder that connects to your existing data source. This approach gives you a proper web interface with access controls while keeping your setup costs low. How do I know when my spreadsheet needs to become an app? Watch for these signals: multiple people editing the same file causing version conflicts, no way to control who sees sensitive data, the file loads slowly or crashes with large datasets, or you're manually emailing updates instead of sharing live data. Any of these means your spreadsheet has hit its limit. Spreadsheet sync vs database migration for turning Excel into an app? Spreadsheet sync keeps your Google Sheets or Airtable intact while adding an app interface on top, which works well for simpler data models. Database migration moves you permanently from spreadsheets into a proper relational database, which handles complex workflows better but requires upfront data modeling. Should I migrate my entire spreadsheet at once or start with one workflow? Start with your most critical workflow, test it thoroughly, then expand. Migrating everything at once increases the risk of broken logic and missed edge cases, while a single-workflow approach lets you run both systems in parallel and catch problems before they affect your whole team.
